name: Rina Dechter
blurb: AI researcher at UC Santa Cruz whose 1986 work contains the early use of the term 'deep learning'.

name: Igor N. Aizenberg
blurb: Tel Aviv University engineer who helped reintroduce the term 'deep learning' to neural networks around 2000.

name: Geoffrey Hinton
blurb: Nobel-winning neural-net pioneer (deep belief nets, backprop) who popularized 'deep learning'; Turing Award laureate.

name: George Cybenko
blurb: Brown University applied mathematician who proved a key Universal Approximation Theorem for one-hidden-layer networks (1989).

name: Kurt Hornik
blurb: University of Vienna statistician who proved multilayer feedforward networks are universal approximators (1989).

name: Maksym Telgarsky
blurb: Stanford researcher who proved ('Representation Wars') that depth can beat width exponentially for some functions.

name: Guido Montúfar
blurb: TU Darmstadt mathematician who showed the number of linear regions of a ReLU net grows exponentially with depth.

name: Kaiming He
blurb: Microsoft Research (now MIT) computer visionist who introduced ResNet residual connections, winning ImageNet 2015.

name: Nelson Elhage
blurb: Anthropic mechanistic-interpretability researcher; co-author of the transformer-circuits 'residual stream' framework.

name: Neel Nanda
blurb: Anthropic interpretability researcher who analyzed 'grokking' mechanistically and co-authored the transformer-circuits framework.

name: Hao Li
blurb: NYU (now NVIDIA) ML researcher; lead author of the loss-landscape visualization work that shapes optimizer analysis.

name: Yann Dauphin
blurb: OpenAI researcher; lead author of the saddle-point problem paper central to high-dimensional optimization.

name: Alethea Power
blurb: DeepMind researcher; lead author of 'Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting' (delayed generalization).

name: Alexander Davies
blurb: University of Toronto ML researcher who unified grokking with the double-descent phenomenon.

name: Mikhail Belkin
blurb: UC San Diego applied mathematician; lead author of the double-descent / overparameterization generalization work.

name: Christian Keup
blurb: Neuroscientist who, with Helias, framed feed-forward ReLU nets as 'origami' that manufacture linear separability.

name: Moritz Helias
blurb: EMBL Heidelberg computational neuroscientist; co-author of the 'Origami in N dimensions' folding theory.

name: Michal Lewandowski
blurb: Researcher who defined the 'space-folding' measure, quantifying how ReLU nets fold input-space paths.

name: Asaf Amrami
blurb: Weizmann Institute researcher who gave a geometric proof that depth beats fixed width for ReLU networks.

name: Yoav Goldberg
blurb: Technion NLP/computational-linguistics professor; co-author of the geometric depth-separation proof with Amrami.

name: Harry Houdini
blurb: Escape artist who turned paper folding and tearing into stage tricks in his 1922 book 'Paper Magic'.

name: Margherita Piazzola Beloch
blurb: Italian mathematician whose 1936 'Beloch fold' lets origami solve the general cubic, trisect angles, double the cube.

name: Koji Huzita
blurb: Japanese origami mathematician who rediscovered (1989) the fold axioms now known as the Huzita-Justin axioms.

name: Robert J. Lang
blurb: Pioneer of computational origami who showed single-fold constructions are complete; built the TreeMaker crease-design tool.

name: Erik Demaine
blurb: MIT professor of computational origami; lead of the fold-and-cut theorem and 'Geometric Folding Algorithms'.

name: Martin Demaine
blurb: MIT professor of computational origami; co-author with Erik Demaine of 'Geometric Folding Algorithms'.

name: Greg Egan
blurb: Australian science-fiction author and programmer who produced the fold-and-cut Koch-snowflake animation.

name: Thomas C. Hull
blurb: Ohio University mathematician and origamist who formalized 'origametry' and the math of the Beloch fold.

name: Martin Grötschel
blurb: TU Berlin / Berlin Institute of Mathematics optimization scholar; author of polyhedral-theory notes underlying ReLU-region analysis.

name: Mor Geva
blurb: AI21 Lab interpretability researcher who showed transformer feed-forward layers act as key-value memories.

name: Ashish Vaswani
blurb: Google researcher; lead author of 'Attention Is All You Need', the Transformer architecture.

name: Karen Simonyan
blurb: Oxford (VGG) / DeepMind computer visionist; lead author of VGGNet, a deep conv-net baseline for ImageNet.

name: Martin Bern
blurb: University of Waterloo combinatorics professor; with Hayes showed deciding flat-foldability is NP-complete (1996).

name: Gregor Hayes
blurb: Combinatorics researcher who with Martin Bern proved flat-foldability is NP-complete (1996).

name: Diederik P. Kingma
blurb: DeepMind researcher; co-inventor of the Adam adaptive-optimizer (with Jimmy Ba) used to train modern networks.

name: Jimmy Ba
blurb: UBC professor; co-inventor of Adam and first author of Layer Normalization, the stabilizer behind transformers.

name: Carl David Tolmé Runge
blurb: Göttingen mathematician whose 1901 interpolation example revealed Runge's phenomenon, the edge oscillation of high-degree fits.

name: Robert Tibshirani
blurb: Stanford biostatistician who introduced the LASSO (1996), the L1 regularizer that yields sparse weights.

name: Arthur E. Hoerl
blurb: University of Oregon statistician who, with Kennard, introduced Ridge Regression (L2) in 1970.

name: Andrei Tikhonov
blurb: Moscow mathematician whose 1943 regularization of ill-posed problems predates and inspired L2/ridge regularization.

name: Nitish Srivastava
blurb: University of Toronto researcher; lead author of Dropout (2014), a key regularizer against overfitting.

name: Josef Hochreiter
blurb: JKU Graz neural-net researcher who first described the vanishing-gradient problem (1991) and later the LSTM.

name: Yoshua Bengio
blurb: Mila / UdeM 'godfather of deep learning'; coined 'vanishing gradient' (1994) and a pillar of modern AI.

name: Rupesh Kumar Srivastava
blurb: Researcher (with Schmidhuber) who introduced Highway Networks (2015), learnable gating on skip connections.

name: Jürgen Schmidhuber
blurb: IDSIA pioneer of recurrent nets and LSTMs; co-author of Highway Networks (2015) that preceded ResNet.

name: Chris Olah
blurb: OpenAI/Distill interpretability researcher; essays on convolutions, manifolds/topology, deconvolution, and Inceptionism.

name: Andrej Karpathy
blurb: Stanford/OpenAI AI researcher; built ConvNetJS, the interactive 2-D classifier used to visualize un-tangling data.

name: Kunihiko Fukushima
blurb: Japanese engineer who invented the Neocognitron (1980), a direct forerunner of convolutional neural networks.

name: David Hubel
blurb: Nobel laureate whose visual-cortex work on receptive fields is the biological blueprint for CNNs.

name: Torsten Wiesel
blurb: Nobel laureate who with Hubel mapped the visual cortex's hierarchy of simple and complex cells.

name: Yann LeCun
blurb: NYU/Meta AI Turing laureate who at Bell Labs built the first deployed CNN for U.S. ZIP-code reading (1989).

name: Irwin Sobel
blurb: Bell Labs engineer who introduced the Sobel gradient filters (1968), classic edge detectors in computer vision.

name: Alex Krizhevsky
blurb: University of Toronto researcher; lead author of AlexNet, the 2012 ImageNet-winning CNN that launched the deep-learning era.

name: Ross Girshick
blurb: Berkeley/FAIR computer visionist; lead author of R-CNN and co-author of YOLO, Mask R-CNN, and MAE.

name: Shaoqing Ren
blurb: FAIR (Meta) computer visionist; co-author of ResNet and lead author of Faster R-CNN (learned region proposals).

name: Joseph Redmon
blurb: University of Washington / Amazon researcher; lead author of YOLO, one-stage real-time object detection.

name: Olaf Ronneberger
blurb: University of Tübingen researcher; lead author of U-Net, the encoder-decoder backbone of biomedical segmentation.

name: Alexander Kirillov
blurb: FAIR (Meta) researcher; lead author of Segment Anything (SAM), the promptable segmentation foundation model.

name: Alexey Dosovitskiy
blurb: Google researcher; lead author of the Vision Transformer (ViT), bringing the transformer to image recognition.

name: Alec Radford
blurb: OpenAI researcher; lead author of GPT and CLIP, which gave vision a text interface via contrastive learning.

name: Gabriel Goh
blurb: Distill/Anthropic interpretability researcher; lead author of the 'multimodal neurons' audit of CLIP.

name: Augustus Odena
blurb: OpenAI researcher; lead author of the Distill essay on deconvolution checkerboard artifacts and the resize-conv fix.

name: Alexander Mordvintsev
blurb: Google researcher; lead author of Inceptionism (2015), turning a frozen net's gradients back into surreal images.

name: U.S. Postal Service
blurb: U.S. mail agency whose ZIP-code reading was the first commercial deployment of a convolutional neural network (LeCun, 1989).

name: Google Inc.
blurb: Technology company whose Research blog published Inceptionism and Inceptionism's CC-licensed image set.

name: University of Brighton
blurb: UK university credited with the folded paper-cranes image used to open the origami chapter.

name: Victoria, Australia
blurb: Australian state named as the location of the stop-sign source image used in the convolution lesson.

name: First deployed CNN for U.S. ZIP-code reading (1989)
blurb: LeCun's backpropagated convolutional network, trained at AT&T Bell Labs, became the first commercially deployed CNN for USPS.
